messages.content:
Hi everyone,

From reading the discussions here, using AI coding assistants (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Copilot, Gemini and so on) during development seems common and widely accepted in this competition. However, I have not seen anyone discuss how this fits with the license and warranty requirements for prizes. A similar license question about models (Section 2.5) came up recently, and Kaggle staff said they could not interpret model licenses under the competition rules, so I am hoping the ARC Prize team can comment on this one. I would also like to hear how others are thinking about it.

What the rules say, as I understand them:

  1. Prize-eligible solutions must be open-sourced. The ARC-AGI-3 page says: "All code and methods must be open sourced to be eligible for prizes." (https://arcprize.org/competitions/2026/arc-agi-3)
  2. The ARC Prize 2026 page says: "all code and methods authored by the submitter must be made open source under a permissive public domain license (eg. CC0 or MIT-0)", and "any 3rd party code or methods not authored by the submitter must be available under, at least, an open source license which allows public sharing (eg. Apache-2.0, GPLv3)." (https://arcprize.org/competitions/2026)
  3. Section 2.5 (Winner License) says winners license "your winning Submission and the source code used to generate the Submission under CC-BY 4.0, an Open Source Initiative-approved license". The Winner License Type at the top of the Rules is also "CC-BY 4.0". Section 2.5 also says: "For generally commercially available software that you used to generate your Submission that is not owned by you, but that can be procured by the Competition Sponsor without undue expense, you do not need to grant the license in the preceding Section for that software."
  4. Section 2.8 (Winner's Obligations) says a winner must "Grant to the Competition Sponsor the license to the winning Submission stated in the Competition Specific Rules above, and represent that you have the unrestricted right to grant that license".
  5. Section 3.14 (Warranty, Indemnity and Release) says: "You warrant that your Submission is your own original work and, as such, you are the sole and exclusive owner and rights holder of the Submission, and you have the right to make the Submission and grant all required licenses."
  6. On tools, Section 2.6.b mentions LLMs and says "the costs of potentially procuring a license for software used to generate a Submission, must also be considered." Section 2.6.c allows automated machine learning tools (AMLT), "provided that the Participant or Team ensures that they have an appropriate license to the AMLT such that they are able to comply with the Competition Rules", and Section 2.8 adds that a Submission made with an AMLT "may win a Prize" but must still meet Sections 2.5, 2.8 and 3.14. None of these clauses names AI coding assistants, so I am not sure how they apply.

Why I am asking:

AI coding tools have their own terms about who owns the generated code. Some assign output rights to the user unconditionally, while others assign them only "subject to your compliance with" their terms, such as account or eligibility conditions. The commercial software exemption in Section 2.5 seems to cover the tool itself, but the code it helps write becomes part of "the source code used to generate the Submission". So a winner may not be fully sure that AI-assisted code is their "own original work", that they are "the sole and exclusive owner and rights holder" of it, or that they have "the unrestricted right to grant that license".

Questions for the ARC Prize team:

  1. For the license and warranty rules (Sections 2.5, 2.8 and 3.14, and the "authored by the submitter" wording on the ARC Prize page), should code written with the help of an AI assistant be treated as the participant's own work, or as third-party code?
  2. Does the commercial software exemption in Section 2.5, or the AMLT clause in Section 2.6.c, apply to AI coding assistants? If so, does it cover only the tool itself, or also the code it helped write?
  3. Do winners need to check the terms of the AI tools they used, or disclose which tools they used?
  4. If there is uncertainty about some AI-assisted parts of a solution, what would you recommend, for example rewriting those parts or noting it in the write-up?
  5. A related point: Section 2.5 calls CC-BY 4.0 "an Open Source Initiative-approved license", but I could not find it on the OSI list (https://opensource.org/licenses), while MIT-0 is listed there. The ARC Prize page asks for CC0 or MIT-0. Which license should winners use for their code, or is either acceptable?

I am asking so that everyone can prepare their open-source release correctly before the deadlines. Thank you!
